Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 35
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Special Education Teacher
  trauma_type: Mugging or robbery
  pcl5: 58

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Authority Presence: Police
  Threat: Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
  Memory: Photographic Recall: Remembering what happened during the frightening event is just like looking at photographs of it in my mind., Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Inadequacy: I am inadequate

Vignette:
Liam Kowalski is a 35-year-old single man of Polish descent who works as a special education teacher at a public elementary school in a mid-sized city. He presented for treatment approximately eight months after being mugged on his way home from a school staff event on a Friday evening in early autumn. He had stayed late to help a colleague prepare materials for the following week and was walking the four blocks to his car when two men approached him from behind. One grabbed him by the collar and shoved him hard into a chain-link fence, wrenching his neck in the process, while the other pressed close and demanded his wallet and phone. Liam complied immediately, handing everything over without resistance. The men ran. The entire encounter lasted perhaps ninety seconds. He stood alone on the pavement afterward, neck aching, hands shaking, and the sound of one of the men shouting the initial demand still ringing in his ears. He did not call the police that night. He told himself he was fine, walked to his car, and drove home.

In the weeks that followed, the memory did not soften. It arrived instead with the quality of still images — the fence's diamond-wire pattern against his cheek, the man's face close to his, the precise angle of the streetlight overhead — each frame exact and unwanted. When these images surfaced, Liam noticed they were accompanied first by a surge of rage so acute it surprised him, and then, almost immediately, by something heavier: guilt. He had come to believe, with a certainty that felt unassailable, that another man — someone more alert, more capable — simply would not have found himself in that situation. He had stayed late. He had walked that route. He had frozen. The guilt and the rage coiled together whenever the memory arrived, and he began to avoid letting his mind go quiet enough for either to find him.

At school, the environment that had once felt like his domain became newly complicated. Liam works with children who sometimes escalate — who shout when frustrated, who cry out without warning. Before the mugging, he had understood this as part of his professional landscape. Now, when a student's voice rose sharply in the classroom, something in his body responded before his mind could intervene: his neck would tighten along the same line of pain from that night, and for a disorienting moment the room around him would collapse and he would be back against the fence, the shouting immediate and close. He had begun positioning himself near the classroom door during group activities, and he catalogued the exits of every space he entered — the gym, the staff room, the school library — within moments of arriving, though he could not have articulated a coherent plan for what he would do with that information.

When a police officer visited the school for a community safety presentation in the spring, Liam spent the duration of the session at the back of the room, unable to attend to what was being said, his body rigid and his attention fixed on the officer's presence in a way that exhausted him. He had not reported the mugging, and the sight of a uniform seemed to press on that fact in ways he found difficult to name. He had come to feel that he was inadequate in some fundamental sense — not merely that he had made a mistake, but that the mistake had revealed something that had always been true about him. He was unable to relax even in his own apartment in the evenings, the stillness feeling less like safety than like exposure.

It was a parent-teacher conference in late spring that finally moved him toward help. A parent raised their voice in frustration during the meeting, and Liam felt himself go somewhere else entirely — not metaphorically, but with the full sensory weight of that Friday night — before returning, shaken, to the conference room. He apologised and ended the meeting early. He sat in his car for twenty minutes afterward. What he most hopes for, he said at intake, is to be able to do his job again without his body treating his classroom like a crime scene. What he is most afraid of is that the person he was before that night no longer exists.
